blocks.text: This is the story of the man who owned the morning, and of the last sunrise he ever shared. The old lord of Eastmere sat in the drafty study, his hands trembling as he signed away his last remaining asset for a handful of silver.

The Merchant did not look at the man, nor did he care for the title of the decaying manor. He reached for the heavy gold signet ring on his thumb, pressing it firmly into a pool of melting red wax upon the parchment.
The ink and seal declared an impossible possession: the eastern sky, the sunrise, and the right to all who look upon it.

He folded the heavy paper into his dark fur-trimmed coat, feeling the solid weight of absolute dominion over the horizon. What is free is never valued, he reminded himself in the quiet room. The following morning, he climbed the ridge with the parchment rolled tightly in his pocket, watching the valley stir beneath him.
He stood before the path where the villagers always gathered, cleared his throat, and made his declaration to the waking air.
From tomorrow, the morning has a price. Rough grey stones rose across the eastern ridge before the frost had left the grass, forming a barrier where the mountain path narrowed.

A single iron gate blocked the ascent, hinged firmly and guarded by the Merchant in his dark coat. At first light, the villagers climbed from their cottages, carrying their wool shawls and stopping cold before the mortar.

The Merchant stood beside an iron bowl, his bronze bell resting on a post. One by one, farmers and weavers reached into their pockets, dropping copper coins into the metal basin with dull clinks. He rang the bell once for each payment, waving them through the narrow bars while his daughter watched from the rear with a troubled frown.
They walked past him in silence, their eyes fixed on the brightening horizon rather than his face.

The coins piled deep in his leather pouch by the time the sun crested the peaks. He watched them gather on the rocks, but the familiar warmth of their laughter had vanished, replaced by the heavy clink of small bronze tokens.

With the chest of copper coins growing heavier each week, the Merchant hired masons to quarry raw granite from the high crags. Above the iron gate, a round stone tower rose layer by layer, casting a long blade of shadow across the narrow trail.
High on the open parapet, he stood above the valley, his dark fur coat snapping in the chill wind as he watched the sun climb over the ridge alone.
Down at the iron bars, his daughter stood in her plain grey dress, her long dark braid resting across her shoulder. She looked up toward the parapet, her eyes bright with concern.
"Open the gate, Father," she called upward, her voice carrying through the cold stone archway. "Let them walk up as they used to. The light belongs to everyone."
The Merchant did not step down. He pressed his gold signet ring into his palm and looked past her toward the distant roofs of Eastmere. "What is free is never valued," he said.

He turned away, pulling the heavy oak door shut behind him with a dull thud. The iron bolt slid into place, locking out the valley below. As summer arrived, a quiet shift took root across the valley floor.

When the first dim purple shadows stretched across the eastern ridge, the villagers did not turn toward the toll gate. Instead, they walked west. They climbed the grassy slopes of the western hill, carrying wooden benches, fresh loaves of rye bread, and paper lanterns suspended from long ash poles.

As the sun sank toward the horizon, the hill bathed in warm copper light. Children chased stray dogs through the high grass while simple wooden flutes filled the warm evening air with slow, wandering melodies.
From his cold stone tower, the Merchant watched the empty toll path. No coins clinked into his iron bowl; no boots rattled the gravel.

Enraged by their silence, he ordered the masons to raise the stone barrier ten courses higher, blocking out the first rays of morning light until even the eastern valley floor lay trapped in grey shadow.

But the villagers never returned to look at his mountain. They had found another horizon that asked for nothing. When autumn turned the leaves to bronze, the Merchant’s daughter walked up the western hill in her plain grey dress, a crown of dried field flowers woven into her dark braid.
The entire village gathered around her as dusk settled over the ridge. Three days earlier, she had walked to the toll gate alone, leaving a folded parchment tucked into the heavy iron lock.
It was an invitation to her wedding, written in her own careful hand. Now, as vows were spoken in the soft amber light, she turned her head briefly toward the eastern peak.

Far across the valley, a dark, solitary silhouette stood high on the tower rampart, motionless against the gathering night. "He won't come," her groom whispered softly, slipping a thin silver band onto her finger.

She looked down at the glowing valley, took her husband's hand, and smiled. High on his cold stone ledge, the Merchant watched the distant lanterns flare to life one by one, holding his gold signet ring tight against his chest as the last warmth of his family slipped into the dark.
Frost stiffened the iron hinges of the gate where no coin had clinked in months.
On a bitter winter dawn, the Merchant slid the heavy bolt back with his own gaunt hands. He reached for the thick hempen rope of the bronze bell and pulled until sound tore across the frozen snow.
He pulled again, his breath turning white in the freezing air, calling out across the valley. Nobody came. No footsteps crunched on the frozen path.

The valley houses remained shuttered and silent, the people having learned to sleep through his cold morning. His arm grew heavy, the rope fell slack, and the stillness settled deep into his chest. Years wore the stone down and rusted the iron gate wide open.
The wall cracked, and moss covered the stones he had laid to divide the world. Every dawn an old man climbed his tower with the legal parchment tucked inside his coat.
Far to the west, lanterns rose and laughter carried across the valley. He never walked there. He owned every sunrise for the rest of his life. He never shared another.
